stimuli.title: Drill Passage 1
stimuli.text:
For years, our school newspaper, the *Eastfield Ledger*, covered pep rallies, cafeteria menus, and the occasional new __teacher, it__ [1] had never broken a real story. That changed last spring, when a sophomore named Priya Nair noticed that every water fountain near the gym was marked out of order. She asked the __principals__ [2] office how long the fountains had been broken, but nobody seemed to know.

__For instance,__ [3] Priya decided to find out for herself. She requested the district's maintenance records, which are open to the public. The stack of work orders that arrived two weeks later __show__ [4] that the fountains had been reported broken eleven times in three years and repaired only once.

Priya spent the next month checking every claim __twice, verifying each one again,__ [5] before she wrote a word. When the facilities manager met with the athletic director to discuss her questions, __he__ [6] admitted that the repair money had gone toward a new scoreboard. __Priya quoted his admission word for word.__ [7] Her finished article drew on three __sources: the work orders,__ [8] interviews with custodians, and the district budget.

The story ran on the front page in May. Within a week, the district __coughed up the cash__ [9] to fix every fountain in the building. Holding one of the first copies off the press, __the story struck Priya as__ [10] proof that a student paper could do more than report scores.

stimuli.title: Drill Passage 2
stimuli.text:
Public swimming pools in the United States began not as places to play but as places to get clean. In the late 1800s, few homes in crowded city neighborhoods had bathtubs, so reformers built public __baths – plain indoor tanks of water –__ [1] where workers could wash for free. The rules posted at the door of each bath __was__ [2] strict: no splashing, no games, and no more than twenty minutes in the water.

__Lifeguards in tall wooden chairs watched over the crowds.__ [3] By the 1920s, the purpose of the pool had changed. Cities were building huge outdoor pools ringed by lawns and __bleachers, some__ [4] held thousands of swimmers at once. Swimming had become a form of recreation rather than a chore.

After World War II, families who moved to the suburbs often built backyard pools of __their__ [5] own, and city pools lost both swimmers and funding. __As a result,__ [6] many of the grand pools built before the war were drained, paved over, or left to crack.

Today, some cities are restoring old pools and building new ones. For my younger brother and __I__ [7], the pool down the street is the center of summer. It gives us a place to cool off, to learn a skill, and __meeting__ [8] neighbors we would never otherwise know. Any child in town can swim all season with a __free pass that costs nothing__ [9]. The reformers who built those first baths wanted cleaner workers, but they ended up giving cities something __way cooler__ [10]: a place where strangers share the same water.

stimuli.title: Drill Passage 3
stimuli.text:
Inside a converted garage at the edge of town, Marisol Vega spends her mornings beside a furnace that never cools below two thousand degrees. The __furnace's__ [1] steady roar is the first thing visitors notice.

Glassblowing looks effortless when Vega does it. She dips a long steel pipe into the molten glass, gathers a glowing blob on its tip, and __blows; gently__ [2] into the other end. The blob swells like a bubble of honey. Turning the pipe constantly, __the glass is kept centered by her__ [3] so that it never sags. Every step must be done __quickly; glass__ [4] that cools unevenly will crack.

Vega learned the craft at nineteen, sweeping floors in a local studio in exchange for lessons. __The owner, Tomas Reyes, let her practice with scraps of glass.__ [5] When Reyes retired and sold the studio to his nephew, __he__ [6] gave Vega his favorite set of tools. The tongs, along with a wooden paddle and a pair of shears, __hangs__ [7] above her bench today, worn smooth by forty years of use.

Vega now sells bowls and vases at craft fairs across the state. __Each piece has a tiny bubble trapped near its base, a flaw she leaves on purpose.__ [8] The bubble, she says, reminds buyers that a person made the piece. She admits that the work is __exhausting and tiring__ [9], but every morning she lights the furnace again, __totally stoked__ [10] to see what the glass will become.

stimuli.title: Drill Passage 4
stimuli.text:
For nearly ninety years, the official weather station in the town of Merrill sat in a grassy lot behind the post office. The daily readings from its thermometer and rain gauge __were__ [1] sent to the national weather service, which used them to track the climate of the region.

Then the town grew around __it, a__ [2] parking lot replaced the grass, and a three-story bank went up next door. Over the years, the __stations__ [3] nighttime readings crept slowly upward. __Eventually,__ [4] meteorologists began to suspect that the station was measuring the town rather than the weather.

To test the idea, the weather service set up a second station in a farm field two miles outside town. Comparing the two sets of numbers, __the pattern was obvious to the researchers.__ [5] The old station – hemmed in by pavement, __brick, and parked cars, ran__ [6] about three degrees warmer at night than the field did. __Its instruments were identical to the ones behind the post office.__ [7]

The meteorologist __whom__ [8] led the study recommended moving the station to the field, but she warned that a move would break the town's long record. To keep the record whole, the weather service ran both stations side by side __at the same time__ [9] for a full year so that old and new readings could be matched. __Merrill's post office was built in 1912 and still has its original clock.__ [10] Today the record continues, and the station measures the weather again.

stimuli.title: Drill Passage 5
stimuli.text:
The summer I turned fifteen, my cousin Dale decided I was old enough to drive the tractor on his family's farm. Dale had been driving it since he was twelve, and he talked about it the way other people talk about riding a __bike, I__ [1] was terrified.

The tractor was older than both of us put together. Its seat – a metal pan with holes punched in __it, was__ [2] hot enough to burn through my jeans by noon. On the first morning, Dale and __me__ [3] drove out to an empty hayfield where I could do no harm. He taught me the three rules his own father had taught __him: keep__ [4] both hands on the wheel, watch the ground ahead, and __always looking__ [5] behind you before you back up.

The first hour went badly. __Behind me, the rows of raked hay finally ran straight.__ [6] I stalled the engine four times and dragged the rake in wobbly loops across the field. __In other words,__ [7] by the afternoon something had clicked. I stopped fighting the wheel and let the tractor do the work.

__Dale told his father that he had never seen a beginner learn so fast.__ [8] I pretended not to hear, but I grinned the whole way home. Now, whenever I visit, Dale hands me the key without a word, and I __hop on that bad boy__ [9] as if I have done it all my life. I still feel a small thrill when the old engine __coughs and rumbles to life__ [10].

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The original joins two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a comma splice. Adding "but" after the comma joins the clauses correctly and signals the contrast between routine coverage and never breaking a story. Choice B removes the comma and creates a run-on, and choice C makes "which" seem to refer to the teacher.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The office belongs to one principal, so the singular possessive "principal's" is needed. Choice C is the plural possessive, which would mean the office of several principals. Choices A and D lack an apostrophe entirely, and "principles" means rules or beliefs.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Priya decides to investigate because nobody could answer her question, so "So" correctly signals a result. "For instance" would introduce an example, but her decision is not an example of nobody knowing. "Likewise" signals similarity and "In other words" signals a restatement, and neither relationship exists here.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular "stack," not "work orders," which is part of the phrase that follows it, and the essay is told in the past tense. "Showed" is past tense and works with a singular subject. Choices A, B and C either use the present tense or a plural verb ("have," "were") that agrees with "orders" instead of "stack."

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Checking a claim "twice" already means verifying it a second time, so the added phrase repeats the idea. "Twice" alone says it once and lets the sentence flow into "before she wrote a word." Choices C and D keep the same kind of repetition in different words.

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Two men are named in the clause, the facilities manager and the athletic director, so "he" could refer to either one. Naming "the manager" makes clear who admitted where the money went, since the facilities manager is the official in charge of repair money. Choice C keeps the ambiguity, and choice D is plural and still unclear.

questions.stem:
[7] The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the underlined sentence:

The new scoreboard can show instant replays and player statistics.

Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it explains why the district chose to buy the scoreboard.
Yes, because it shows that the repair money was well spent.
No, because it contradicts the manager's admission about the repair money.
No, because it adds a detail about the scoreboard that distracts from the account of Priya's reporting.
questions.explanation: The paragraph describes how carefully Priya reported her story, and the scoreboard's features have nothing to do with that. The sentence should not be added because it pulls attention away from her reporting. It does not contradict the manager, so choice C gives a false reason, and choices A and B claim purposes the sentence does not serve.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: A colon correctly follows the complete clause "Her finished article drew on three sources" and introduces the list of those sources. A semicolon (choice C) must join two independent clauses, and the list is not one. Choice D wrongly uses a semicolon between items in a simple list, and choice B makes the list hard to separate from the rest of the sentence.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is most consistent with the style and tone of the essay?
questions.explanation: The essay is written in a clear, straightforward style, and "found the money" matches it. "Coughed up the cash" and "forked over the dough" are too slangy for the rest of the essay. Choice D swings the other way into stiff, inflated wording.

questions.stem: [10] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: the story seemed to Priya to be
it seemed to Priya that the story was
questions.explanation: The opening phrase "Holding one of the first copies off the press" must describe the subject that follows it. Only Priya can hold a copy, so the subject must be "Priya," as in choice D. Choices A and B make "the story" the one holding the copy, and choice C makes the subject "it," which cannot hold anything either.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: baths, plain indoor tanks of water –
baths – plain indoor tanks of water,
baths: plain indoor tanks of water;
questions.explanation: The phrase "plain indoor tanks of water" interrupts the sentence to define the baths, and it is correctly set off by a matching pair of dashes. Choices B and C mix a comma with a dash, and an interrupting phrase must open and close with the same mark. Choice D puts a semicolon before "where workers could wash," which is not an independent clause.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "rules"; "posted at the door of each bath" is a phrase that describes them. A plural subject needs the plural verb "were," which also keeps the past tense of the paragraph. "Was," "is" and "has been" are all singular and agree with "bath" by mistake.

questions.stem: [3] The best placement for the underlined sentence would be:
options: at the end of the paragraph.
questions.explanation: "The crowds" needs something to refer to, and the paragraph first mentions large numbers of people when it says the pools "held thousands of swimmers at once." Placing the sentence right after that mention ties the lifeguards to those crowds. At the end of the paragraph (choice D), it would separate "the crowds" from the swimmers and interrupt the paragraph's closing point about recreation.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Some held thousands of swimmers at once" is an independent clause, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma creates a comma splice. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses. Choice B removes the comma and creates a run-on, and choice C still joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The pools belong to the families, so the possessive pronoun "their" is correct. "They're" is a contraction of "they are," and "there" refers to a place. "Their's" is never correct, because possessive pronouns do not take apostrophes.

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: City pools lost swimmers and money, and the closing of many pools followed from that loss. "As a result" correctly signals cause and effect. "Nevertheless" and "In contrast" signal an opposite outcome, which does not fit, and "Similarly" implies a comparison the sentence does not make.

questions.stem: [7] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of the preposition "for," so it must be in the object case: "me." Removing "my younger brother and" shows the test: "For me" is correct, but "For I" is not. "Myself" is reflexive and needs an earlier "I" in the sentence, and "mine" is possessive.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The series begins with two infinitives, "to cool off" and "to learn a skill," so the third item must also be an infinitive: "to meet." "Meeting" and "for meeting" break the pattern with a different form, and "they meet" turns the last item into a clause.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: A free pass by definition costs nothing, so "that costs nothing" repeats the idea. "Free pass" says it once. Choices C and D add the same kind of repetition ("at no cost," "complimentary").

questions.stem: [10] Which choice is most consistent with the style and tone of the essay?
options: of a more durable and enduring nature
questions.explanation: "More lasting" fits the thoughtful, informative style of the essay and leads naturally to the colon and the idea that follows. "Way cooler" and "super awesome" are too casual for the essay. Choice D is wordy and repeats itself, since "durable" and "enduring" mean the same thing.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The roar belongs to one furnace, so the singular possessive "furnace's" is correct. "Furnaces" is a plain plural with no possession, and "furnaces'" would mean several furnaces. "Furnace is" makes the sentence ungrammatical.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Blows gently into the other end" is the last item in a series of three actions, so no punctuation belongs between the verb and its adverb. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "gently into the other end" is not one. Choice B creates a fragment, and choice D uses a colon where nothing is being introduced.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The phrase "Turning the pipe constantly" describes Vega, so the subject right after the comma must be "she." Choice D puts Vega in that position. Choices A, B and C all make "the glass" the subject, which suggests the glass is turning the pipe.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Both "Every step must be done quickly" and "glass that cools unevenly will crack" are independent clauses, and a semicolon correctly joins them. Choice B joins them with only a comma, which is a comma splice, and choice C joins them with no punctuation, a run-on. Choice D puts a semicolon before a dependent clause beginning with "because."

questions.stem:
[5] The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the underlined sentence:

He warned her that she would break a hundred pieces before she made one worth keeping.

Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it adds a detail about Reyes's teaching that fits the paragraph's account of how Vega learned the craft.
Yes, because it explains why Vega chose glassblowing over other crafts.
No, because it contradicts the earlier claim that glassblowing looks effortless.
No, because the paragraph has already said how many pieces Vega broke.
questions.explanation: The paragraph tells how Vega learned from Reyes, and his warning adds a vivid detail about that apprenticeship. The sentence should be added. It does not contradict the earlier paragraph, which says the craft looks effortless only when Vega, now an expert, does it, and the paragraph never says how many pieces she broke, so choices C and D are wrong.

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Two men are named before the pronoun, so "he" could mean Reyes or his nephew. The context shows it was Reyes: he was retiring, and the tools were worn by forty years of use, which fits the longtime owner rather than the nephew who had just bought the studio. "They" is plural and still unclear.

questions.stem: [7] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "tongs." The phrase "along with a wooden paddle and a pair of shears" adds information but does not change the subject, so the verb must be the plural "hang." "Hangs," "is hanging" and "has hung" are all singular forms.

questions.stem: [8] The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it explains how Vega traps a bubble inside the glass.
Kept, because it introduces the bubble that the next sentence explains.
Deleted, because it contradicts the claim that Vega's pieces sell well.
Deleted, because it shifts the paragraph's focus away from craft fairs.
questions.explanation: The next sentence begins "The bubble, she says," which only makes sense if the bubble has already been introduced. The underlined sentence should be kept because it sets up that explanation. Choice A is wrong because the sentence never explains how the bubble is made.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Exhausting" and "tiring" mean nearly the same thing, so using both is redundant. "Exhausting" alone says it once and says it more strongly. Choices B and D repeat the same idea in other words.

questions.stem: [10] Which choice is most consistent with the style and tone of the essay?
options: in a state of anticipatory eagerness
questions.explanation: The essay is written in a clear, admiring style, and "eager" fits it. "Totally stoked" and "mad hyped" are slang that clashes with the rest of the profile. Choice C is stiff and wordy.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural "readings"; "from its thermometer and rain gauge" is a phrase that describes them. The plural verb "were" agrees with "readings" and keeps the past tense. "Was," "has been" and "is" are singular and agree with "gauge" by mistake.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Then the town grew around it" and "a parking lot replaced the grass" are both independent clauses, so a comma alone cannot join them. A period separates them into two sentences. Choice B is a run-on, and choice D turns the second clause into a garbled relative clause.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The readings belong to one station, so the singular possessive "station's" is needed. "Stations'" is plural possessive, but the paragraph is about a single station. "Stations" has no apostrophe at all, and "station is" makes the sentence ungrammatical.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The suspicion comes after years of readings creeping upward, so "Eventually" correctly marks the passage of time. "For example" would present the suspicion as an example of rising readings, and "Similarly" signals a comparison. "Otherwise" suggests an alternative that the paragraph never sets up.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: an obvious pattern emerged for the researchers.
it was obvious to the researchers that a pattern existed.
the researchers saw an obvious pattern.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase "Comparing the two sets of numbers" must describe the subject that follows it, and only the researchers did the comparing. Choice D makes "the researchers" the subject. Choices A, B and C make "the pattern" or "it" the subject, as if those had compared the numbers.

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The phrase "hemmed in by pavement, brick, and parked cars" interrupts the sentence and opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash. Choice B supplies the matching dash. Choice C leaves the interruption open, and choice D puts a semicolon between the subject and its verb.

questions.stem: [7] The best placement for the underlined sentence would be:
options: at the beginning of the paragraph.
after the sentence ending "obvious to the researchers."
questions.explanation: "Its instruments" must refer to the second station, and the point that its instruments matched the old ones explains why the comparison was fair. That belongs right after the sentence that introduces the second station in the farm field. Where it is now, "Its" seems to refer to the old station, which would compare the station with itself.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of the verb "led," so the subject form "who" is needed. "Whom" is the object form and would fit only if the meteorologist received the action. "Which" is not used for people, and "whose" is possessive.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Side by side" already says the two stations ran together, so "at the same time" adds nothing. Deleting it leaves a clear sentence: the stations ran side by side for a full year. Choices B and C keep the repetition and add more of it.

questions.stem: [10] The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it gives the history of the building where the station first stood.
Kept, because it explains why the station had to be moved.
Deleted, because it adds a detail about the post office that has nothing to do with keeping the weather record whole.
Deleted, because it repeats information given in the first paragraph.
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains how the town kept its weather record unbroken, and the age of the post office and its clock have nothing to do with that. The sentence should be deleted. Choice D gives the wrong reason, because the first paragraph never mentions when the post office was built.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by only a comma, which is a comma splice. Adding "but" joins them correctly and shows the contrast between Dale's ease and the writer's fear. Choice B is a run-on, and choice D adds a comma that leaves the splice in place.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The phrase "a metal pan with holes punched in it" interrupts the sentence and opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash before the verb "was." Choice D supplies that dash. Choice A mixes a dash with a comma, choice B leaves the interruption unclosed, and choice C puts a semicolon between the subject and its verb.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject of the verb "drove," so it must be the subject form "I." Removing "Dale and" shows the test: "I drove" is correct, but "me drove" is not. "Myself" is reflexive and needs an earlier "I" in the sentence.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The clause "He taught me the three rules his own father had taught him" is complete, and a colon correctly introduces the list of rules that follows. A semicolon (choice B) needs an independent clause on each side, and the list is not one. Choices C and D fail to separate the clause from the list clearly.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The rules are commands in a series: "keep both hands," "watch the ground," and so the third must be "always look." "Always looking" is a different verb form that breaks the pattern. Choices B and D also break the series, one by adding a subject and one by using an infinitive.

questions.stem: [6] The best placement for the underlined sentence would be:
options: at the beginning of the paragraph.
after the sentence ending "across the field."
after the sentence ending "do the work."
questions.explanation: "Finally" signals the result of learning, so the sentence belongs after the writer stops fighting the wheel and lets the tractor do the work. Where it is now, and after the sentence about wobbly loops, it would claim straight rows during the hour that went badly. At the beginning of the paragraph, it would announce success before the struggle is described.

questions.stem: [7] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The paragraph turns from a bad first hour to success later in the day, so a contrast is needed. "Even so" shows that things improved despite the stalling and wobbly loops. "In other words" signals a restatement, "For instance" an example, and "Similarly" a comparison, and none of those fits the turn.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Dale told his father that they had never seen a beginner learn so fast.
Dale told his father that he had never seen a beginner learn so fast himself.
Dale told his father, "I have never seen a beginner learn so fast."
questions.explanation: In the original, "he" could mean Dale or his father. Quoting Dale directly makes clear that Dale is the one who had never seen a beginner learn so fast. Choice C adds "himself" but still leaves "he" ambiguous, and choice B uses a plural pronoun that is just as unclear.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is most consistent with the style and tone of the essay?
questions.explanation: The essay is personal but not slangy, and "climb into the seat" fits that plain, descriptive voice. "Hop on that bad boy" and "jump on the thing" are too casual and vague. Choice C is stiff and formal for a personal story.

questions.stem: [10] Given that all the choices are true, which one most vividly describes the sound of the old engine starting?
questions.explanation: "Coughs and rumbles to life" gives the reader a sound to hear and makes the old engine seem almost alive, which fits the warm ending. "Starts," "turns on" and "begins to operate" are accurate but say nothing about how the engine sounds. The question asks for the most vivid description, so the original is best.
